newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia jet fuel, diesel unfazed by low Western price.
newsitem.headline: Asia jet fuel, diesel unfazed by low Western price.

text.p: Asian jet fuel and diesel prices show little signs of softening until the end of the year despite a sharp drop in Western prices and the current weakness of the crude market, industry sources said on Tuesday.
A series of substantial purchases of jet fuel and diesel big Asian buyers such as China, India and Indonesia have kept prices strong, traders said.
"The Singapore market is holding very well. It is trading independently of London," said Tom James, Asia-Pacific regional manager, Natural Resources, at Credit Lyonnais Rouse Derivatives.
The regional buying spree began when Indonesia more than doubled its November diesel and jet fuel imports to 700,000-800,000 tonnes and 200,000 tonnes respectively, traders said.
Subsequently, India surprised the market and bought 520,000 tonnes of diesel for December arrival compared with nothing in November and 120,000 tonnes in October.
India is expected to maintain its purchase level for January, but Indonesia's December demand is not likely to match that of November, traders said.
China raised its diesel and jet fuel purchases for the winter because of low inventories brought on by lower refinery runs, traders said.
"China reduced their refinery runs in November due to the high price of imported crude then," one trader said.
Higher diesel imports from China are also expected because of a reduction in the import tariff from six percent to three percent, they said.

Japan, Asia's largest jet fuel consumer during the winter, has not entered the market in a substantial way. It bought about four cargoes for November and five 30,000-tonne cargoes for December, a far cry from the tens of cargoes it purchased on a spot basis last winter, traders said.
Japanese purchases would solely depend on how cold the weather would be, one trader said.
Asia's large appetite was clearly seen earlier this month when it absorbed at least 300,000 tonnes of diesel and jet fuel exported from the United States and Europe for arrival in December.

The export of these Western cargoes was made possible when Asian diesel prices soared to trade at about $15 per tonne above European prices, which made it profitable for traders to ship cargoes east, one industry source said.
Diesel prices peaked on November 13 in Singapore, trading at a five-year high of $30.80 a barrel on a free-on-board (fob) basis. It is currently quoted about 20 cents below this mark.
At about the same time, jet fuel traded at $30.95 a barrel fob Singapore, its highest since last winter.

These high prices are in contrast to declining prices in the West, where front-month gas oil futures traded on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) fell from a five-year peak of $247 per tonne in October to settle on Monday at $218.75.
Similarly, front-month Brent crude futures on the IPE fell from a post-Gulf War record of $25.06 a barrel in October to close on Monday at $22.87.
Traders said the downtrend on crude prices has not ended, but felt that unless they fell below $22 a barrel, jet fuel and diesel prices in Asia would be unfazed.
